transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-18
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Cole (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Lina Park (Aurora Head of ML), Daniel Ortiz (Aurora Platform Eng), Sofia Reyes (CFO)
---
[00:00] Ethan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm Ethan, AE on the Redwood account, and Maya is our SE who will run the Optimize walkthrough.
[00:18] Maya: hey all, hi Lina, Daniel, Sofia. I'll jump in with the plan: we'll walk batching basics, prefix or KV cache recommendations for your summarization flows, and then show a simple cost model. lots of Q&A welcome.
[00:36] Lina: thanks, excited. quick context: we run nightly summarization of support tickets and a live assistant for agents. latency target for live assist is <150ms p99, and cost matters — we've got 10M monthly queries.
[00:58] Daniel: also to add, traffic is bursty at shift changes, and we prefer VPC/private deployment if possible for compliance.
[01:12] Sophia: hi, i'm mostly here to understand pricing impact and potential capex vs opex.
[01:25] Maya: got it. i'll start with batching. at a high level, batching increases GPU utilization by grouping requests, but increases tail latency. Redwood Optimize suggests per-route batching windows: for low-latency routes (live assist) we keep micro-batches ~8-12ms window or disable batching; for high-throughput offline jobs we use larger windows up to 30-50ms or async batch pipelines.
[01:52] Ethan: to add, our runtime supports continuous batching which helps with latency-sensitive batching because it streams tokens while adding new requests to the batch.
[02:06] Daniel: couple questions — how does continuous batching interact with KV cache? our live assistant will have many repeated prefixes.
[02:18] Maya: great question. prefix / KV cache stores attention key/value states for repeated prefixes (e.g., system prompt + user history). when cache hit rate is high, you skip re-computing prefix tokens and only run decoding for the new tokens, saving compute. with continuous batching, we can still batch decode steps; cache reduces per-request compute significantly.
[02:44] Lina: how do you estimate hit rates? our sessions are 8-12 messages average, but agents often edit prompts.
[02:54] Maya: typical approach is sample request traces, cluster similar prompt prefixes, and estimate hit-rate — for ticket summarization we often see 40-60% prefix reuse within a short time window if prompts are templated. for live agent sessions it's lower maybe 20-30% unless you pin system prompts.
[03:16] Ethan: note that for Aurora's nightly summarization (batch job) we expect very high hit-rate if you prefix with the same system prompt + template. that’s where KV cache gives large wins.
[03:30] Daniel: ok, numbers please — what's the cost delta?
[03:34] Maya: i'll go through a simplified cost model. assumptions: model ~redwood-llm-13b-quant (hypothetical), token price compute unit X, baseline no-cache run: average request 1,200 tokens (prefix 900 + new 300). with no cache and small batches the per-token GPU time is T, so cost per request ~ $0.045. with KV cache hit on prefix you avoid recomputing 900 tokens, so cost drops to compute for 300 new tokens + cache overhead ~ $0.012-0.015 per request. that's ~3x improvement.
[04:14] Sofia: that seems big — are those numbers realistic or optimistic?
[04:18] Maya: they're illustrative; real numbers require your traffic trace. we'll run the 48h benchmark. some caveats: cache hit also increases memory (KV storage) and slightly longer warmup when populating cache. plus not all prompts will hit.
[04:33] Ethan: we also have quantization and kernel selection effects — from our tests moving 13B to 8-bit quant reduces perf by 1.2-1.4x in latency but cuts cost. Optimize suggests per-route quant profiles.
[04:50] Lina: for the live assistant we can't accept >150ms p99 — so sounds like we can't enable big batching there, but KV cache might still help?
[04:59] Maya: exactly. for the live route we recommend: keep batching window minimal (micro-batching), enable prefix caching aggressively for pinned system prompts, and use continuous batching to keep throughput without sacrificing decode latency. that typically keeps p99 under threshold while lowering cost by 20-40% depending on hit rate.
[05:18] Daniel: network wise, if we go Private Dedicated, will the cache be local per GPU cluster or a central service? implications for VPC egress?
[05:28] Maya: with Redwood Dedicated / Private, KV cache is colocated with the runtime instance; there's an in-memory store sharded across GPUs. no egress to public internet. we'll provide network topology diagram in the security pack.
[05:42] Ethan: and for hosted routes we serve cache within our tenancy but with strict isolation; we have SOC2 and can support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for encryption at rest.
[05:54] Sofia: ok please send the SOC2 and KMS details.
[05:59] Lina: any tradeoffs between caching vs model distillation/shorter prompts? we've tried prompt compression but it's lossy.
[06:09] Maya: caching and prompt engineering are complementary. compression reduces tokens but may hurt quality; caching preserves full prefix quality while saving compute for repeated prefixes. sometimes we combine modest compression with caching for best economics.
[06:23] Daniel: can Redwood do automatic cache invalidation if user context changes? we have sensitive PII concerns and need TTL and manual invalidation hooks.
[06:33] Maya: yes TTLs, explicit delete APIs, and namespace separation. plus RBAC so only your service tokens can manage cache keys. we'll include API examples in the follow-up.
[06:47] Ethan: let's go through a quick worked example — assume 10M monthly requests; baseline no-cache cost at $0.045 leads to $450k/month. with 50% effective cache hit on prefixes you reduce to ~$225k - plus smaller overhead for cache memory and ops. even 25% hit saves ~112k/month.
[07:18] Sofia: those are big numbers — what's the pilot scope?
[07:21] Maya: pilot: we spin up a dedicated test cluster or use hosted with a controlled routing policy, run your trace for 48h, measure p50/p95/p99, cache hit-rate, and token cost. deliverables: benchmark report, tuned batching windows per route, and cost model spreadsheet.
[07:39] Lina: timeline? we'd like results before budgeting cycle in early december.
[07:44] Ethan: we can start benchmark config this week, run the 48h within next two weeks and deliver by 2026-11-30.
[07:52] Daniel: about security again — will you need data exfiltration access to our logs?
[07:57] Maya: we only need hashed traces; we support on-prem agents to run benchmarks if you prefer zero data leaving your VPC.
[08:07] Lina: perfect.
[08:10] [08:10] Ethan: quick demo — Maya will share screen to show Optimize console presets for batching and KV cache.
[08:18] Maya: on screen — this is the route panel; you can set batch window (ms), max-batch-size, and a cache policy (prefix-only or full-message). you can also see an estimated cost delta based on sample token distributions (note: estimate uses our runtime perf profiles).
[08:38] Maya: here is a sample: route "live-assist": batch window 8ms, max-batch-size 16, cache prefix-only, TTL 5 minutes. estimated cost reduction 18% for their sample traffic. route "nightly-summary": batch window 50ms, max-batch-size 128, cache full-message, TTL 24h, estimated cost reduction 70% due to high reuse.
[09:02] Daniel: console also shows a per-token time breakdown?
[09:06] Maya: yes token-level compute + kernel overhead + memory swap (if cold) and estimated network time. we include percentile latency and a simulated cost model.
[09:18] Lina: any gotchas when using longer TTLs and multi-tenant caches?
[09:24] Maya: make sure to namespace keys per customer/user to avoid collisions. for multi-tenant hosted we isolate caches per account. for Dedicated you can shard by customer id. long TTL increases memory but improves hit-rate.
[09:38] Sofia: ok finance-level question — what's the pilot price/commitment?
[09:43] Ethan: pilot pricing is typically usage-based plus a small professional services fee for benchmark setup. i'll follow up with a SOW and pilot pricing options: hosted trial or a short Dedicated proof-of-concept.
[09:56] Lina: any blockers we should be aware of?
[09:59] Maya: main blocker is access to representative traces and a list of pinned prompts/system messages. also network policy for test agents if you want private workload.
[10:10] Ethan: cool. we'll note next steps: Ethan to send pricing and SOW, Maya to prep benchmark config and cost model, Aurora to send sample traces.
[10:22] Daniel: will you also include suggested quantization profile? we run mostly fp16 today.
[10:28] Maya: yes we include quantization options per route — e.g., 8-bit for offline batch jobs, 16-bit for live routes to keep p99 low. we'll show kernel-level perf numbers in the report.
[10:40] Lina: one last quick: do you have pre-built integrations for our alerting and tracing? we use Datadog and the standard OpenTelemetry stack.
[10:48] Ethan: yes, Redwood Console has tracing hooks and token-level latency logs that export to Datadog/OTel. we can also add custom metrics.
[10:58] Sofia: ok sounds good.
[11:00] [wrap up] Ethan: thanks everyone, action items in chat. we'll aim to get the benchmark running this week. any final questions?
[11:08] Lina: none, thanks.
[11:11] Daniel: thanks all.
[11:13] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up with the deck and security pack.
[11:18] Ethan: end meeting.
